en: If you're building your own AI agent, or if
you're building any other piece of software
that uses AI internally, for example, to
generate text, to generate responses to
customer support emails, or anything like
that, you may want to consider adding evals
to your project.
Eval, short for evaluations, are systematic
tests used to measure whether an AI model or
a complete AI system, an agent, for example,
behaves according to specified capability,
quality, safety, reliability, or product
requirements.
In case you have a software engineering
background, you may think of evals as
integration tests for AI models.
The idea is that you're building something
that, let's say, is producing responses to
customer requests, and you have another
model evaluate some test run results. So you
simply generate some dummy customer request
emails, for example. You let your piece of
software then generate answers, and you let
another AI model then score these answers,
for example.
For example, that is what evals are about—
evaluations of the performance of a large
language model in a specific environment and
use case.
Therefore, evals can be quite expensive
because you not only have your system
do its work, which
leverages AI, for which you typically pay
money, of course. But instead, you also
often have an additional model judge the
output, which costs money again. So evals
tend to be rather expensive, but depending
on what you're building, they are important
nonetheless because they give you an
automated way of testing outputs generated
by large language models.
